newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch minister says watchdog report inadequate.
newsitem.headline: Dutch minister says watchdog report inadequate.

text.p: Dutch Economics Minister Hans Wijers said on Wednesday a critical report by the Dutch Audit Office on state aid to troubled companies was "inadequate in many ways" and in some cases even suggestive.

"Our main objection is that the Audit Office surveyors seem to have operated within a constructed reality which does not mesh with the factual, economic and legal context of the investigated operations," Wijers said in a letter to parliament.
The watchdog said the Dutch government had failed to apply rules set by parliament for state support and in some cases had not properly reported aid to the European Commission.

Wijers, who wrote the letter also on behalf of Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm, said the Audit Office had overlooked the fact that all cases surveyed were exceptional and therefore needed tailor-made solutions.

"In all cases the negotiation and decision processes were quite complex, actions and reactions of the parties involved could not be predicted and widely diverging interests played a role," Wijers said.
He said the watchdog's claim that parliament had been insufficiently informed in some cases did not do justice to the extensive information that was sent to parliament.

But because the information usually contained confidential corporate items and it could make the government's own position in the negotiations vulnerable most of the close and intensive contacts with parliament had a confidential character, Wijers said.
The minister said he regretted the statement that he and his predecessors had repeatedly failed to inform parliament.
"We consider this (accusation) to be inaccurate given the fact that the Audit Office acknowledges it does not have the information which is necessary to draw a conclusion," he said.
Wijers also said the European Commission (EC) had been informed in all cases where this was necessary.
He said the watchdog's conclusion that a so-called "techno-lease construction" for aircraft maker Fokker in 1994 had been a form of government support was incorrect.
Through this deal Fokker sold its technological know-how to Dutch Rabobank which then received tax benefits from the state. Wijers said the techno-lease deal was a matter of applying regular laws.
"Given the implications the (watchdog's) qualification 'provision of support' might get in a European context, a more careful conclusion would have shown wisdom," Wijers said.
The minister said the watchdog's conclusion that, given the support sums that were provided in recent years, the state had lost sight of the costs per saved job was irrelevant.

"In all cases surveyed, a recovery of profitability was the main goal," Wijers said, adding that such operations should not be primarily judged on their direct effects on employment and therefore costs per job.
He said the government had asked the Audit Office to keep several parts of its report confidential and regretted the watchdog had declined to do so.
The Audit Office investigated five cases in the years 1987-1994 where the Dutch provided aid to aircraft maker Fokker, car manufacturer NedCar and truckmaker DAF.
The Dutch state is currently in talks about selling the bankrupt aircraft company's manufacturing activities to Korea's Samsung Aerospace.
Nedcar was saved after Sweden's Volvo and Mitsubishi Motors Corp each took a one-third stake with the Dutch state retaining the remaining third.
DAF NV went bankrupt in 1993 but its unlisted and slimmed-down survivor DAF Trucks emerged from the ashes and posted a net profit of 164 million guilders last year.
Earlier this month, U.S. truck maker Paccar Inc said it had made a 933 million guilders friendly bid to take over DAF Trucks from the Dutch state and financial institutions who now own the firm.
-- Theo Kolker, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000
